notes: Holyoake heads a single-party National government; template coalition slot 2 holds the Social Credit Political League as the centrist third force (MD also puts a centrist party there). CPNZ was pro-Beijing in 1970, so it sits in 19; the pro-Moscow Socialist Unity Party takes slot 4. Rātana movement in 14 (church-based politics outside the blocs), Federation of Labour in 18, Federated Farmers in 15. Icons only for National and Labour (same orgs as MD sprites).

0.name: New Zealand Security Intelligence Service
0.text:
The New Zealand Security Intelligence Service received its present name and a statutory basis in 1969, having operated as the Security Service since 1956. Its Director, Brigadier Herbert Gilbert, reports directly to the Prime Minister and works closely with ASIO, MI5 and the CIA.

Its officers monitor the Communist and Socialist Unity parties, waterfront unions, anti-war protesters and Soviet-bloc visitors, and the new act has drawn loud protest from civil libertarians. It has no constituency, but in a security crisis it would supply the government with the lists, the files and the arguments.

1.name: New Zealand National Party
1.text:
The New Zealand National Party has governed since 1960 and won a fourth successive term in November 1969. Prime Minister Keith Holyoake, a Motueka farmer and party leader since 1957, presides over a cabinet in which Jack Marshall is Deputy Prime Minister and Robert Muldoon holds Finance.

National stands for private enterprise, farm exports, stable government and loyalty to the ANZUS and SEATO alliances, with a small New Zealand force in Vietnam. Holyoake's consensus style keeps the party broad, but Britain's approach to the European Community threatens the farm economy its rural and business base depends on.

2.name: Social Credit Political League
2.text:
The Social Credit Political League is New Zealand's third party, founded in 1953 on the monetary theories of C. H. Douglas. It won its first seat when leader Vernon Cracknell took Hobson in 1966, but lost it in November 1969 despite gaining more than nine percent of the vote.

It offers itself as a moderate alternative to the two big parties: cheap state credit for housing and development, relief for small business and farmers, and an end to the power of the trading banks. Its supporters are small-town shopkeepers, farmers and protest voters, and its leverage lies in splitting the vote in marginal seats.

3.name: New Zealand Labour Party
3.text:
The New Zealand Labour Party, which built the welfare state under Michael Joseph Savage, has been in opposition since 1960 and lost narrowly again in 1969. Its leader since 1965 is Norman Kirk, a self-taught former engine driver from Kaiapoi with a powerful presence, who is reshaping the party into a credible government.

Labour promises full employment, more state housing, a fairer deal for Māori and Pacific Islanders, and an independent foreign policy that would bring the troops home from Vietnam and oppose French nuclear tests. Its base is the unions, the cities and the Māori seats.

4.name: Socialist Unity Party
4.text:
The Socialist Unity Party was founded in 1966 by members who left the Communist Party of New Zealand when it sided with Beijing. Loyal to Moscow, it is small but well placed in the unions, with the Auckland drivers' leader Bill Andersen among its leading figures.

It calls for withdrawal from Vietnam and SEATO, nationalisation of key industries, workers' unity within the Federation of Labour and friendship with the socialist countries. It contests elections without success, but its leverage lies in the trades councils of Auckland and Wellington and the industrial disputes it can lead.

5.name: Progressive Youth Movement
5.text:
The Progressive Youth Movement is a radical student and youth network formed in the late 1960s and active in Auckland, Christchurch and Wellington. It mixes Marxists, anarchists and pacifists, and stages the most confrontational demonstrations against the Vietnam War, apartheid sport and visiting American dignitaries.

It calls for immediate withdrawal from Vietnam, an end to SEATO and ANZUS, and a socialist society built from below. It despises Labour's caution and the old communist parties alike. Its leverage lies on the streets and the campuses, where it can turn any official visit into a running battle with the police.

6.name: New Zealand Manufacturers' Federation
6.text:
The New Zealand Manufacturers' Federation speaks for the factories that have grown up behind import licensing and high tariffs since the 1930s. Its members range from Auckland appliance assemblers to textile mills and car assembly plants that depend on a protected home market.

It defends import controls, local content rules and state support for industry against the free-traders in Treasury and among the farmers, and warns that opening to Australian and Asian goods would destroy jobs. Its leverage lies in the employment it provides, its ties to both parties and its influence over the import licensing schedules.

7.name: New Zealand–USSR Society
7.text:
The New Zealand–USSR Society promotes friendship with the Soviet Union through films, exchanges, language classes and tours. Its activists come from the Socialist Unity Party, the Labour left and the waterfront and drivers' unions, and it works closely with the Soviet mission in Wellington.

It presents the USSR as a partner for peace and trade, a buyer of New Zealand wool and butter, and campaigns against SEATO, ANZUS and the Vietnam War. Its membership is small and watched by the Security Intelligence Service, but it gives Moscow a respectable voice in New Zealand public life.

8.name: Anjuman-i Husayni
8.text:
Anjuman-i Husayni is a small gathering of Shia Muslims of Indian and Fiji Indian origin in Auckland who meet in private homes to commemorate Muharram and teach their children. Many trace their faith to Gujarat and to the Shia communities of Fiji and East Africa.

Its members are shopkeepers, clerks and students who hope to build a first Shia centre and keep religious instruction alive. Moderate and loyal, they avoid politics, though they follow the debates of reformist clerics in Iraq and Lebanon. Their weight lies in close family ties and links to relatives in Suva, Bombay and Nairobi.

9.name: Majlis-i Najaf
9.text:
Majlis-i Najaf is a tiny group of Iranian and Iraqi students at the universities of Auckland and Canterbury who pass around the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965. They meet discreetly, aware that the Shah's agents keep watch on students abroad.

They reject the Pahlavi monarchy, Ba'athist Iraq and Western domination, and hold that only government by the Islamic jurists can bring justice. They have no public presence in New Zealand, but they are disciplined, mobile and tied to student networks in Britain, Europe and the Gulf.

10.name: New Zealand Muslim Association
10.text:
The New Zealand Muslim Association was founded in Auckland in 1950 by Gujarati Muslims and post-war refugees from Europe, and is the country's oldest Muslim body. It runs a small prayer house in Ponsonby and is raising funds for a proper mosque.

Its leaders are conservative, respectable and loyal to the Crown, keeping out of politics and seeking good relations with the authorities. They look to the Muslim World League and Gulf donors for books, imams and money, and their leverage lies in being the recognised voice of a community of a few hundred families.

11.name: Shabab al-Khilafa
11.text:
Shabab al-Khilafa is a handful of Arab and Malaysian students in Auckland and Wellington drawn to the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, whose pamphlets reach them from Beirut and Amman. They meet in closed study circles and keep apart from the established Muslim association.

They reject nationalism, democracy and both Cold War blocs, and call for a single caliphate to unite all Muslims under Islamic law. They have no presence beyond the campuses, but their certainty and their links to the party's networks abroad make them the most uncompromising voice among New Zealand's young Muslims.

12.name: Halaqah Pelajar
12.text:
Halaqah Pelajar are the weekly study circles of Malaysian and Indonesian Colombo Plan students in Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin. Inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood and by Mawdudi's Jamaat-e-Islami, they read the Qur'an and the works of Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in English and Malay.

They seek to form a disciplined Islamic elite that will return home to reform society through preaching and education, and they reject both communism and Western permissiveness. Their footprint in New Zealand is small, but they shape the future engineers, teachers and officials of Southeast Asia.

13.name: The Treasury
13.text:
The New Zealand Treasury, under Secretary Henry Lang, is the dominant department in Wellington. It controls the budget, external borrowing and the import licensing debate, and its economists advise Finance Minister Robert Muldoon, whose own ambitions often collide with official advice.

The Treasury stands for fiscal discipline, export-led growth and the gradual liberalisation of a heavily regulated economy, and it fears the effect of British entry into Europe. Its leverage lies in the budget, its near monopoly on economic information and a network of officials who expect to outlast governments.

14.name: Te Haahi Rātana
14.text:
The Rātana movement is the Māori church founded by the prophet Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana in the 1920s, with its headquarters at Rātana Pā near Whanganui. Since its alliance with Labour in 1936 its members have held the Māori seats in Parliament.

It combines Christian faith with the demand that the Treaty of Waitangi be honoured, Māori land protected and Māori welfare improved. It is socially conservative, wary of radical protest and loyal to its covenant with Labour. Its leverage lies in its congregations across the North Island and its hold on the Māori electorates.

15.name: Federated Farmers of New Zealand
15.text:
Federated Farmers of New Zealand, formed in 1946, is the voice of the country's sheep, dairy and beef farmers, whose exports earn most of the nation's foreign exchange. Its provincial executives are dominated by large runholders and prosperous dairy farmers.

It demands guaranteed access to the British market, lower costs for farm inputs, fewer union stoppages on the waterfront and in the freezing works, and a strong say over the producer boards. Many of its leaders sit in the National caucus, and its leverage lies in the export economy itself: when the farmers suffer, the country suffers.

16.name: Associated Chambers of Commerce of New Zealand
16.english: Associated Chambers of Commerce of New Zealand
16.text:
The Associated Chambers of Commerce of New Zealand federates the business chambers of Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin and the provincial towns. Its members are importers, retailers and merchants who chafe at import licensing and price controls.

It calls for freer trade, lower taxes, deregulation of the economy and an end to compulsory unionism, and it is suspicious of both Labour's planning and National's interventionism. It has no seats, but its submissions to select committees, its press statements and its weight in the National Party give it a steady voice.

17.name: Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society of New Zealand
17.english: Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society of New Zealand
17.text:
The Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society, founded in 1923, is New Zealand's oldest conservation body and has gained new energy from the fight over Lake Manapouri, which the government plans to raise to power the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter. Its members are naturalists, trampers, teachers and students.

It calls for the protection of native forests and birds, more national parks and the preservation of Manapouri's shoreline, and it lobbies Parliament and the press. Respectable and non-partisan, it is cautious about mass protest, but the Manapouri campaign is turning conservation into a national political issue.

18.name: New Zealand Federation of Labour
18.text:
The New Zealand Federation of Labour, founded in 1937, is the central body of the country's trade unions, made strong by compulsory unionism and the arbitration system. Its president since 1959, Tom Skinner, is a pragmatic anti-communist who deals directly with both Holyoake and Kirk.

It defends the arbitration court, general wage orders, full employment and the closed shop, and is linked to the Labour Party through affiliated unions. Militant unions on the waterfront and in the freezing works push it leftward, but its leverage lies in its power to call or prevent national stoppages.

19.name: Communist Party of New Zealand
19.text:
The Communist Party of New Zealand, founded in 1921, is the only Western communist party whose majority sided with Beijing in the Sino-Soviet split. General Secretary Vic Wilcox leads a small, disciplined party that publishes the People's Voice and keeps close ties with China and Albania.

It follows Mao Zedong Thought, denounces Soviet revisionism and American imperialism alike, and calls for revolutionary struggle against monopoly capital. Its influence lies in a few unions and among young radicals drawn to the Cultural Revolution, but its rigid line limits its growth.

20.name: Keep Politics Out of Sport
20.text:
Keep Politics Out of Sport is the cry of the rugby clubs, provincial unions and letter-writers who back the 1970 All Black tour of South Africa, on which Māori players will travel as 'honorary whites'. The New Zealand Rugby Football Union and many National supporters stand behind it.

It defends sporting ties with South Africa, resents anti-apartheid protesters and long-haired students, and voices a provincial, egalitarian nationalism suspicious of intellectuals, unions and outside interference. It has no organisation of its own, but rugby is the national religion and its anger can move votes.

21.name: National Socialist Party of New Zealand
21.english: National Socialist Party of New Zealand
21.text:
The National Socialist Party of New Zealand was founded in 1969 by Colin King-Ansell, who had earlier been jailed for an attempt to firebomb an Auckland synagogue. It is a tiny uniformed group modelled on the American Nazi Party.

It preaches white supremacy, antisemitism and violent anti-communism, opposes Polynesian immigration and defends apartheid South Africa. It has no electoral support and is shunned even by most of the right, but its stunts and provocations attract press attention and police surveillance.
21.wiki: National Socialist Party of New Zealand

22.name: New Zealand Army
22.text:
The New Zealand Army maintains infantry companies and an artillery battery in South Vietnam within the Australian task force, and a battalion in Malaysia and Singapore. Lieutenant General Sir Leonard Thornton, Chief of Defence Staff since 1965, oversees the three services under a single Ministry of Defence.

The officer corps is small, professional and loyal to the Crown, committed to forward defence alongside Australia, Britain and the United States. It has no political tradition whatsoever, but in an emergency it is the only organised force beyond the police that the state could call upon.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Elizabeth II is Queen of New Zealand, represented by Governor-General Sir Arthur Porritt, a surgeon and Olympic medallist and the first New Zealand-born holder of the office. The Queen is due to visit this year for the Cook bicentenary celebrations.

Monarchists see the Crown as the bond with Britain and the Commonwealth, the guarantor of parliamentary government and, for many Māori, the partner in the Treaty of Waitangi. Their support is broad among older Pākehā and rural voters, the Returned Services' Association and the National Party, though the Crown itself stays above politics.
